title: Ames and Pierre du Moulin the son: full certainty is supreme degree, not essential form
source_text: XXXIV. Similiter Amesius, Perkinsii vestigiis insistens, & respiciens ad assensum specialem, quo aliquis apprehendit gratiae jam factae possessionem actualem, dicit Particularem istam certiorationem intellectus interdum falsam deesse, ad tempus, qui tamen veram fidem in cordibus suis habent interim latentem, & ita docere experientiam. In Medulla Theologiae, cap. 3. num. ultimo; & in Bell. enervato concedit non omnes justificatos mox esse certos de sua justificatione, lib. 6. de Justit. cap. 1. n. 11. Sed praesertim in hanc sententiam clare & aperte concedit Petrus Molinaeus, Petri Molinaei filius, Theologiae Doctor, & praebendarius Cantuariensis, piis animabus notus libro perutili de Pace animae, aliisque piis operibus Gallice ab ipso editis. De quo tamen contemptim loquitur, & quem cum Ludovico Molinaeo ipsius fratre imprudenter confundit scriptor ille qui Reformatis imputat, quod doctrina sua de Justificatione, Christianam Ethicen subvertant. Is igitur, tractatu Gallico de forma sive natura fidei justificantis, docet fidem justificantem non satis accurate & prudenter definiri per firmam fiduciam, & plenam certitudinem, qua fidelis credit peccata sibi esse per Christum remissa; quia firma illa & plena certitudo, de propria salute & remissione peccatorum suorum, notat quidem fidei supremum gradum, & summam perfectionem, non tamen fidei formam essentialem, quae potius in his tribus consistit, 1. Ut Christi merita amplectamur; 2. Ut ea nobis appropriemus, & nostra faciamus; 3. Ut extra ipsum salutem non quaeramus, secundum quod habet Belgica Confessio, asserens veram Fidem esse, quae Jesum Christum cum omnibus suis meritis amplectitur, illumque sibi ceu proprium effectum vindicat, nihilque deinceps extra illum quaerit. Art. 22.
pass_a_gloss: Similarly Ames, following Perkins's footsteps, and looking to the special assent by which someone apprehends the actual possession of grace already made, says that that particular assurance of the intellect is sometimes falsely absent for a time in those who nevertheless have true faith meantime latent in their hearts, and that experience so teaches. In the Marrow of Theology, chapter 3, last number; and in Bellarmine Enervated he concedes that not all the justified are at once certain of their justification, book 6 on Justification, chapter 1, number 11. But especially into this opinion clearly and openly concedes Peter du Moulin, son of Peter du Moulin, Doctor of Theology and prebendary of Canterbury, known to pious souls by a most useful book on the Peace of the Soul, and other pious works published by him in French. Of whom nevertheless that writer speaks contemptuously, and whom he imprudently confounds with Louis du Moulin his brother — the writer who imputes to the Reformed that by their doctrine of Justification they subvert Christian ethics. He therefore, in a French treatise on the form or nature of justifying faith, teaches that justifying faith is not defined accurately and prudently enough by firm trust and full certainty by which the faithful believes sins to have been remitted to him through Christ; because that firm and full certainty concerning his own salvation and the remission of his sins marks indeed the supreme degree of faith and its highest perfection, yet not the essential form of faith, which rather consists in these three: 1. That we embrace Christ's merits; 2. That we appropriate them to ourselves and make them ours; 3. That we seek salvation nowhere outside Him — according to what the Belgic Confession has, asserting that true Faith is that which embraces Jesus Christ with all His merits, and claims Him to itself as its proper effect, and thereafter seeks nothing outside Him. Article 22.
pass_b_english: Ames: particular intellectual assurance of grace already possessed can be falsely absent for a time while true faith lies latent.
Not all justified are at once certain of justification (Bell. Enerv. VI).
Pierre du Moulin the son (Canterbury): full fiducia that ‘my sins are remitted’ = supreme degree, not essential form.
Essential form: embrace Christ’s merits; appropriate them; seek salvation nowhere else — Belgic Confession art. 22.
